definition.text: A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it: the client sends the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions.

facts.text: Instead of connecting directly to a server that can fulfil a request, the client directs the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions.
The indirection controls complexity or adds benefits such as load balancing, privacy or security; proxies were devised to add structure and encapsulation to distributed systems.
A proxy may sit on the user's own computer or at any point between the user's computer and the destination servers.
Proxies typically filter requests, log requests, or transform them by adding or removing headers, encrypting or decrypting, or compressing.
A proxy that passes requests and responses on unmodified is usually called a gateway or sometimes a tunneling proxy.
A web proxy receives an ordinary HTTP request except that the full URL, not just the path, is passed; it makes the request and returns the response.

Proxies may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For, or the standardised Forwarded field, to pass on client information, but these should not be trusted blindly: they may be absent, modified or added by several proxies.
A proxy works at layer 7 of the OSI model; network address translation is similar but works at layer 3, so it is less resource-intensive and less flexible.

definition.text: A forward proxy is a server that sits in front of a group of client machines and communicates with Internet servers on their behalf.

facts.text: When the clients request sites and services on the Internet, the forward proxy intercepts the requests and communicates with the web servers on their behalf, like a middleman.
A forward proxy sits in front of the client so that no origin server ever communicates directly with that client.
It can regulate traffic by preset policies, convert and mask client IP addresses, enforce security protocols and block unknown traffic, strengthening policy enforcement inside an internal network.
Common uses are blocking access to certain content, reaching geo-restricted content, providing anonymity and avoiding other browsing restrictions.
A content-filtering proxy gives administrative control over content relayed through it, is used by organizations to enforce acceptable use policy, and often supports user authentication and logging.
An open proxy is a forwarding proxy accessible by any Internet user; an anonymous proxy reveals that it is a proxy but does not disclose the client's originating IP address.
Web filtering proxies cannot see inside HTTPS unless managed clients are configured to trust a root certificate whose private key the proxy knows.
Proxies bring anonymity but can still track personal information, and setting up and maintaining one can be costly and requires configuration.

title: Transparent proxy
article: Proxy server#Implementations of proxies > Transparent proxy

definition.text: A transparent or intercepting proxy redirects or filters client traffic without being explicitly selected by the client.

facts.text: It is often deployed without browser or application proxy settings, so clients may be unaware that their traffic passes through a proxy.
It sits in the network path and commonly redirects outgoing TCP port 80 traffic; older HTTP terminology used 'transparent proxy' for a proxy that did not modify requests or responses.

Businesses use intercepting proxies to enforce acceptable use policies without configuring client browsers, and ISPs in some countries use them to save upstream bandwidth and improve response times by caching.
Interception raises problems: the original destination IP and port must reach the proxy, HTTP authentication such as NTLM breaks, and some requests and responses become uncacheable by a shared cache.

definition.text: A caching proxy speeds up requests by returning content saved from an earlier request by the same or another client.

facts.text: Caching proxies were the first kind of proxy server, and web proxies are commonly used to cache web pages from a web server.

Keeping local copies of frequently requested resources lets large organizations significantly cut upstream bandwidth use and costs while significantly increasing performance; most ISPs and large businesses have one.
Poorly implemented caching proxies can cause problems, such as an inability to use user authentication.
A Performance Enhancing Proxy mitigates link problems, for example improving TCP performance under high round-trip times or packet loss, by merging TCP ACKs or compressing application-layer data.

definition.text: An API gateway is an API management tool that sits between clients and a set of backend services as their single entry point, enforcing security and throttling policies before passing requests on.

facts.text: It is a single entry point into a system that encapsulates the internal architecture and provides an API tailored to each client.
It receives API requests, enforces throttling and security policies, passes requests to the back-end service and returns the result to the client.
Microservices typically expose fine-grained APIs unlike what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to multiple services; a gateway gives all clients a single entry point.
Core functions are routing requests to the appropriate backend service, load balancing, and API composition, which combines several backend API requests into one frontend request.
Security and traffic control features include authentication and authorization, data encryption, rate limiting and throttling, and IP whitelisting or blacklisting.
Resilience and visibility features include retry and circuit breaking, caching, and monitoring, logging, tracing and analytics.
Advantages: it encapsulates the internal structure of the API, gives a centralized view of the API and simplifies client code.
Disadvantages: a possible single point of failure, a possible performance impact, a bottleneck if not scaled properly, and challenging configuration.

definition.text: An API gateway handles each request in stages: it validates the request, checks identity and rate limits, routes it to a service and deals with errors.

facts.text: The client sends an HTTP request to the gateway, which parses and validates the request's attributes and performs allow-list and deny-list checks.
The gateway talks to an identity provider for authentication and authorization, then applies rate limiting rules and rejects the request if it is over the limit.
Once the request has passed the basic checks, the gateway finds the relevant service by path matching, transforms the request into the appropriate protocol and sends it to the backend microservices.
The gateway can handle errors and use circuit breaking for faults that take longer to recover, can use the ELK stack for logging and monitoring, and sometimes caches data.

definition.text: The Backend For Frontend pattern creates a separate backend service for each specific frontend application or interface.

facts.text: It avoids customizing a single backend for multiple interfaces.
Microservice output is often not in the exact format or filtering a front end needs; BFF moves that reformatting logic from the frontend into an intermediate layer.
Its primary function is to get the required data from the appropriate service, format it and send it to the frontend; GraphQL performs really well as a BFF.

Consider it when a shared general-purpose backend carries significant development overhead, when the backend should be optimized for one client, or when customizations accommodate multiple interfaces.

title: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer

definition.text: A reverse proxy, an API gateway and a load balancer are three components that sit in front of servers, each suited to a different job (hiding and protecting servers, routing to services, spreading traffic), and a system can use all three together.

facts.text: A reverse proxy keeps servers hidden from clients and shields sensitive websites from cyber-attacks.
An API gateway delivers requests to the right services and suits busy applications with many intercommunicating services.
A load balancer directs traffic evenly across servers to prevent bottlenecks and is essential for popular websites with heavy traffic.
A load balancer is useful when multiple servers serve the same function; a reverse proxy is useful even with one server, and can also act as a load balancer, but not the other way around.

title: Reverse proxy

definition.text: A reverse proxy, or surrogate server, is a proxy server that appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests to one or more ordinary web servers.

facts.text: The reverse proxy returns the original server's response as if it came from the proxy itself, so the client never learns of the original server.

It sits in front of the origin servers so no client communicates with them directly; the web servers can be hidden behind a firewall on the internal network with only the reverse proxy exposed to the Internet.
A forward proxy serves clients restricted to a private network that need public Internet resources, whereas a reverse proxy is used to protect the servers.

By inspecting HTTP headers it can present a single IP address to the Internet while relaying requests to different internal servers by URL, rewriting URLs where needed, and can balance load across servers.

It often terminates TLS connections from clients, which centralises certificate management, access control, logging and routing and reduces TLS work on backend servers; it can also compress content to speed up loading.
It can cache static and dynamic content (web acceleration), satisfying a considerable number of requests and greatly reducing the load on origin servers.
In spoon-feeding, a dynamically generated page is served to the proxy in full and fed to the slow client as the connection allows, so the generating program need not stay open.

Application firewall features can protect against DoS and DDoS attacks, and it can add authentication to a server that has none, but it gives no protection against attacks on the web application itself.

related: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer

definition.text: Putting a reverse proxy in front of servers adds complexity and creates a single point of failure and a high-value security target.

facts.text: A reverse proxy is a single point of failure for the back ends it fronts: misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable, and adding failover proxies increases complexity further.

To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic the proxy must decrypt and re-encrypt it, which needs the TLS certificate and private key, extends the number of systems with access to unencrypted data and makes it a more valuable attack target.
Giving a third party's reverse proxy access to private keys places confidentiality, integrity and availability in that party's hands.

It can track request IP addresses and read or modify unencrypted traffic, so anyone who compromises it can do the same; exposing internal applications not hardened to public standards through it may increase the attack surface.
